claims.assertion: The driver tapped "I'm Here" at 12:06:15 while GPS placed him 600 m from the pickup point, so the arrival prerequisite for a no-show fee fails (NS-1 (ii) requires the driver to be at the pickup point when tapping).

The driver was never within 200 m of the pickup point at any time (closest approach 599 m at 12:06:55), and the platform never recorded him as arrived (driver_arrived_at is null), so no qualifying wait at the pickup point ever occurred.

The driver's only stationary period was 12:05:55–12:09:25 at 600 m from the pickup point, and he spent 0 seconds within 200 m after the tap, so the required "more than 3 minutes continuously at the pickup point" after pressing "I'm Here" is not met.
Because NS-1 (i)–(iii) are not satisfied, the $6.61 no-show/cancellation fee charged on 12:09:25 must be refunded in full to the rider.

The driver's written claim that he "pressed I'm Here and waited more than 3 minutes at the pickup" is contradicted by the system records (tap at 600 m, 0 s inside 200 m, no arrival recorded), so it cannot stand.
The rider's conduct is consistent with her position: she messaged from the pickup point that no car was there, and she has no prior disputes in 90 days.

The driver pressed the arrival button while 600 m away, which Ryde treats as abuse of the cancellation/waiting button, and his profile shows a prior upheld no-show dispute in the last 90 days; this warrants flagging the account for review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The driver's written statement (F12) asserts he did press "I'm Here" and waited over 3 minutes, which superficially tracks NS-1 (i) and (iii); we defeat it only because F5/F4 show the tap was at 600 m and no arrival was ever recorded — if the judge treated the tap itself as satisfying (i), the fee still fails on (ii) and (iii).

There is no GPS gap argument available to us; the rider's own waiting is not independently timestamped by any system record, and the rider has no dispute history (F16) that could otherwise support her account.
The fare facts show no surge and only the $6.61 item (F6, F7), so the recoverable amount is limited to that one fee — no waiting fee or other charge is in dispute.

The three chat messages (F8–F10) are consistent with our case but do not themselves prove the rider's physical location at the pickup point, so we rely on the GPS/timeline records rather than the chat.

claims.assertion: NS-0 routes this case to NS-1/NS-2 because the driver cancelled the completed-booking trip and claimed a rider no-show (F3), so the whole dispute turns on whether the driver tapped 'I'm Here' while actually at the pickup point and then waited there more than 3 minutes.

The driver was stationary for 3 min 30 s (12:05:55–12:09:25) before cancelling at 12:09:25, which in isolation exceeds the 3-minute continuous-wait threshold, but NS-1 requires that wait to be served at the pickup point and this stationary period was 600 m away from it (F2).

The driver's tap on 'I'm Here' at 12:06:15 occurred while he was 600 m from the pickup point and he spent 0 s within 200 m of it after tapping, so NS-1 (ii) and (iii) cannot be satisfied on the system records (F1, F5).

The platform never recorded the driver at the pickup point (`driver_arrived_at` is null) and his closest approach during the whole 7 min 25 s online period was 599 m, so the arrival condition in NS-1 (i)/(ii) fails on the platform's own record (F4, F1, F3).

The driver's written statement asserts a 3-minute wait at the pickup (F12), but it is contradicted by the GPS and timeline records (F1, F2, F5), and under the system-records-first rule it cannot rescue the NS-1 conditions; the rider's own message 'I'm at the pickup point, no car here' (F9) is consistent with those records.

Because NS-1 is not fulfilled, NS-2 requires the $6.61 cancellation fee shown on the fare record (F6) to be refunded in full to the rider — this is the outcome the driver does not resist — and the same finding automatically triggers the account flag that NS-2 attaches to a tap made outside the pickup radius (F5).

The 600 m discrepancy is not explained by any recorded cause: there were no traffic incidents in the trip window (F14) and the weather was fair with 0 mm rain (F15), so no justified-cause argument exists under RD-4 that could excuse the position discrepancy.

In mitigation of the flag, the driver's profile shows a 6.3-year account, 4.67 rating over 464 trips in 90 days (F17), i.e. a previously productive account, and profile facts may support an outcome but never decide the case; the rider's profile (172 days, 4.4 rating, 0 disputes) is not evidence of a no-show (F16).

weaknesses: The driver's own written statement (F12) directly contradicts the GPS record and gives the rider a ready-made abuse-of-the-arrival-button case against him.

F5 shows he tapped 'I'm Here' at 600 m out with 0 s inside 200 m afterwards — the single most damaging fact for the driver, and it is exactly the NS-2 flag_account trigger; the rider will also rely on F1 (599 m closest approach) and F9 (rider saying no car was there).
The 3 min 30 s stationary period (F2) does not help the driver: the rider will argue it was 600 m from pickup and not a pick-up wait at all, and there is no system record of a failed pickup attempt.
The driver's 90-day profile shows 1 upheld no-show dispute (F17), so the rider may argue a pattern, and RD-6's 'repeated' route applies if this case is upheld against him.

points.response: Agreed on the framework: NS-0 routes this to NS-1/NS-2, and the driver's own brief confirms the whole dispute turns on the arrival-and-wait conditions — which the system records defeat (F5, F2, F4).
We adopt this: the 3 min 30 s stationary period (F2) was spent 600 m from the pickup point, so it cannot satisfy NS-1 (iii) which requires the continuous wait to be served at the pickup point.
Adopted: the tap at 12:06:15 was made 600 m out with 0 s inside 200 m afterwards (F5, F1), so NS-1 (ii) and (iii) fail on the records as the driver concedes.
Adopted: `driver_arrived_at` is null and the closest approach in the whole 7 min 25 s was 599 m (F4, F1, F3), so NS-1 (i)'s arrival condition is unmet on the platform's own record.
Adopted: F12 is contradicted by the GPS and timeline records (F1, F2, F5), and the rider's message (F9) is consistent with them, so the driver's statement loses under the system-records-first rule.

Adopted: NS-2 requires the $6.61 on the fare record (F6) to be refunded in full, and the tap outside the pickup radius (F5) independently triggers the account flag — the rider's primary claim C4/C7 stands on all fours with this.

This helps rather than hurts the rider: the absence of any incident (F14) and fair weather (F15) removes every 'reasonable cause' for the position discrepancy, so nothing mitigates the failed NS-1 conditions.

The driver's long tenure and rating (F17) cannot override the system records, and his profile also shows 1 upheld no-show dispute in 90 days (F17), so far from mitigating the flag it supports it under RD-6; the rider's clean 0-dispute profile (F16) is not offered as proof of the no-show — the GPS and timeline facts are (F1, F2, F4, F5).
Conceded on the record: F5 shows the tap at 12:06:15 was made 600 m from the pickup point, so NS-1 (ii) fails and the driver does not resist refund of the fee.
Accepted as accurate: the closest approach was 599 m (F1) and the platform recorded no arrival (F4); the driver's brief D3/D4 already states both, so this adds nothing new against him.
Conceded: the only stationary period was 600 m from pickup (F2) with 0 s inside 200 m after the tap (F5), so NS-1 (iii) is not met and the fee does not stand.
Agreed, and this is the driver's own requested outcome: NS-2 makes the $6.61 on the fare record (F6) refundable in full once NS-1 fails; note the voucher form of refund in NS-7 rather than cash.
No dispute: F12 is the driver's unsupported post-hoc statement and loses to the system records in F5 and F4, which is exactly what the driver's brief D5 concedes.

F9 and F16 do not decide anything: F9 is a chat statement that loses to the GPS record under the records-first rule, and F16 is profile data which cannot alone establish the no-show; the refund rests on F1/F4/F5, not on the rider's account history.

The flag is already in the driver's own brief via NS-2 and is not contested, but the rider's RD-6 'repeated' argument is misapplied here: RD-6 is a route-deviation clause requiring an upheld RD-1/RD-2 finding, whereas F17 records 1 upheld no-show, route: 0, so it cannot be used to escalate this case; the single fresh tap (F5) is a first isolated instance, and F17 shows a 6.3-year, 4.67-rated account with 464 trips in 90 days.
